description: The largest manzanita of the foothills, a crooked shrub or small tree 2-6 m tall with smooth, polished red-brown bark and bright green oval leaves; white to pink urn-shaped flowers hang in clusters from late winter. It grows in chaparral and open oak woodland on the lower slopes, and its mealy red-brown berries feed bears, foxes, coyotes, jays and quail through the summer.

season_notes.winter: Flowering from February: drooping clusters of small white to pink urns, the first nectar of the year for hummingbirds and bees.
season_notes.spring: The last flowers fall in April and green berries swell; new leaves are a fresh, slightly bronzed green.
season_notes.summer: Berries ripen red-brown, and the thin outer bark peels in curls from the red trunks.
season_notes.fall: Evergreen through the dry season; next winter's flower buds already hang at the branch tips.

notes: Common manzanita is the tallest manzanita of the western Sierra foothills, 2-6 m, sometimes a small tree, in chaparral and open blue oak and foothill pine woodland on the lower slopes, often beside whiteleaf manzanita. It has no burl and does not resprout: fire kills it and its seed, stored in the soil, comes back. Grown from whiteleaf manzanita (arctostaphylos_viscida.json) with what differs changed. Size: height_m 2-5 for the file and an 'old' class to 6.5 m with thicker trunks (trunk_radius 1.3) and a bare base (base_size 0.25), the small-tree form; stems 3-6, fewer and heavier than whiteleaf's, with a little lean and a chance of a fork. Bark the same polished red-brown (bark_rgb a shade darker), pattern smooth, stems and limbs sinuous as in A. viscida. Leaves 2-5 cm, oval to elliptic, bright green and a little glossy on both sides, not glaucous: leaf_shape 'oval' (not round_vertical) with orientation 'outward' and roll_deg 55, because the leaves are held more loosely than whiteleaf's vertical, edge-on leaves; ao_min 0.76 (lower than whiteleaf's 0.8) since a green crown shows more inner shade than a pale one. The limbs start low (start 0.08, foliage start 0.1, clumps along the limbs with tip_bias 0.9) following the polish of the foothill shrubs, so the crown is not a bare-skirted ball. Flowers white to pink urns in drooping panicles February-April (months [2, 4], seasons winter and spring); berries 8-12 mm, mealy, ripening red-brown June-September. Architectural model Leeuwenberg (provisional), as for A. viscida: each shoot ends in an inflorescence and growth carries on from buds below it, which gives the forked, crooked branching. Leaf colour, crown ratios and card density are first guesses for the lineup.
